newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Bund, BTPs vols dip as EMU tensions ease.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Bund, BTPs vols dip as EMU tensions ease.

text.p: Implied volatility of German and Italian debt options on LIFFE inched lower on Wednesday as impending U.S. jobs data replaced European single currency as the market's chief concern, brokers said on Wednesday.

Volume was thin as April non-farm payrolls loomed on Friday, sending players to the sidelines. Meanwhile, the battle over the Bundesbank's gold eased after Bonn said funds from the asset revaluation would be transferred to the government in 1998 instead of this year.
"Very little is happening," a trader at a U.S. bank in London said. "(BTP) vol has come off as usual."
The trader quoted implied volatility of September BTP options at around 7.8 percent compared with around 8.0 percent at the close on Tuesday and 8.4 percent last week.
He said trades were slightly bearish, amid dwindling expectations for an Italian interest rate cut, despite a drop in inflation to 1.6 percent in May, its lowest level since February 1969.
The data was at the top end of expectations and coupled with weekend comments from Bank of Italy Governor Antonio that the flames of inflation have not been extinguished, the tone was negative.
A European bank executed a covered combo, buying September puts at 128.00, selling calls at 131.00 and buying upside calls at 133.00 for around 8,000 lots.
"They're open on the downside but covered on the upside," he said.
By 1400 GMT, September BTP futures were quoted at 130.35, down 56 basis points on the day.
Implied volatility of July Bund options dipped to around 5.42 percent versus 5.80 percent on Tuesday. August and September options were little changed at 5.42 and 5.59 percent respectively.
June Bund futures, which expire on Thursday, were quoted at 101.30, down 15 basis points while September Bunds were quoted at 100.25, down 0.15.
"Elliott Wave analysis points the Bunds up but it seems to be trickling the downside at the moment," the trader at the U.S. bank said.
A trader at a French bank in London also said volatility dipped.
"A lot of exciting news we've been waiting on tenterhooks to hear has come out," he said. But he did not expect levels to push too much lower.
"The locals wouldn't want the vols to drop too far. They are probably still a bit too short," he said.
